title: Buying SPY on RSI under 30 won 26 of 34 trades and finished $34,600 behind holding
author: person-person12
selftext:
Buying oversold is probably the most agreed-on idea in retail trading. RSI drops under 30, you buy, you wait for it to come back up. I wanted to know what 25 years of doing exactly that actually pays out, so I ran it on SPY daily candles from January 2001 to the end of March 2026, ten grand to start, sell on the first close back above 50.

It fired 34 times in 25 years and won 26 of them, so a **76% win rate**, and the money it made across those trades came to about two and a half times the money it lost. By every number people normally post, thats a good strategy. It turned $10,000 into $16,035.

Holding SPY across the same window turned $10,000 into $50,654. So the oversold rule finished about **$34,600 behind doing nothing at all** while winning three quarters of its trades. Costs were charged in both runs, 3 cents a share of slippage and 50 cents commission each side, and they came to $192 across all 34 trades, so thats not what did it either.

**\_\_\_\_**

The reason is sitting in the trade count. 34 trades across 6,348 trading days means the rule owned SPY for a thin slice of those 25 years and sat in cash for the rest of it, waiting on a reading that mostly never came. Almost everything SPY did happened while the rule was watching from the sidelines, and you cant collect money you werent in the market for.

Its a bit like only turning up to work on the days you feel sharp. Your average day looks fantastic and your paycheque is still small, because the pay comes from the days you showed up.

**\_\_\_\_**

Now the part id want somebody to say if this was my rule getting pulled apart, because it did do one thing well. Holding SPY straight through gave back **56.5%** at the worst point, which is 2008 in a single number, and the oversold version never gave back more than **29.3%**. If sitting through a halving is the thing that makes you sell at the bottom, then cutting that roughly in half is worth something, and some people would take it on purpose.

Where it falls apart is how its usually sold. Nobody posts RSI under 30 as a way of owning less of the market for a quarter of the century, they post it as an edge, and the high win rate is the whole reason it reads like one. Both of these ran on the same candles, the same window and the same costs in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading), so the only thing separating $16,035 from $50,654 is how much of those 25 years the money was actually in.

comments.author: SuperOrbital_Trading
comments.body: Yeah, sitting out 90% of the time is a huge compounding miss. And only 34 trades in 25 years is pretty gross. I would be curious at looking at the trade cadence personally. As an options trader, that to me looks like an interesting factor as a possible indicator for trading leaps.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: The cadence is the part i found interesting, theyre barely spread out at all. Daily SPY closing with RSI under 30 clusters into crisis windows, so you get a handful of entries around 2008 and 2020 and then years of nothing in between. Your leaps angle is worth more because of that, a signal that only fires in a panic does a lot more for an options position than a share one.

comments.author: wsxedcrf
comments.body: Mean reversion strategies are all about how you handle the extreme cases.  At RSI 30, you buy, and if SPY goes lower, do you buy more? and what if it goes even lower, you will have a threshold, the greater the tolerence, the higher the return, the higher the max DD

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: This is the right question and the version i ran doesnt scale in at all, one entry at RSI 30 and thats it. Tiering it is the obvious next test, 30 then 25 then 20 with a third of the size at each. **Ill run it,** id rather post the number than argue about it.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
That's the crux of it. The tolerance setting is really a sizing decision, and the trade-off you describe is real: more scaling in means more return and a deeper drawdown, because you're putting the most capital to work at the moment things look worst. What's worth checking is whether the extra return is just extra exposure, rather than better timing. If you compare it at the same average time in market, or the same max drawdown, the scaled version often looks a lot less special.

The other catch is sample size. With 34 trades, the extreme cases are probably only a handful of episodes, and 2008 and 2020 would dominate the result. Scaling in worked there because the market recovered, and a rule tuned on those two events tells you little about the next one that doesn't.

It might help to separate the dips by cause, like a routine pullback versus a systemic event such as Lehman or COVID. The right amount to scale in for those two can be very different. Cymetica's EventTrader has pre-tagged event context that could help label those episodes.

Do you cap the total position, or let it keep adding as price falls?

comments.author: TurbulentStiffness
comments.body: win rate means nothing when you leave cash sitting idle on the sidelines for decades. you basically just traded away compounding returns to avoid holding through bear markets.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Youre right and thats the bit a win rate hides. 26 of 34 winners and it sat in cash for most of the window, so it didnt get beaten on the trades, it got **beaten on all the time it wasnt holding anything.**
